question: At what cervical dilatation is the first stage of labor considered complete?
explanation: The first stage of labor spans from true labor onset until the cervix reaches full dilatation, which is measured as ten centimeters. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why must the upper part of the uterus contract while the lower part stays relaxed during labor?

options.A: To push the fetus downward while pulling the cervix open
options.B: To prevent the placenta from detaching too early in labor
options.C: To keep the amniotic fluid enclosed inside the lower segment
options.D: To stop maternal blood pressure from dropping during contractions

explanation: Active contraction of the upper segment generates the force needed to push the baby down, while the passive lower segment and cervix stretch to allow passage. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which specific protein builds up in the uterine muscle to help electrical impulses spread across the whole uterus?
explanation: Connexin-43 forms gap junctions that connect myometrial cells electrically so the uterus can contract together as a single unit. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of calcium inside uterine muscle cells during a contraction?

options.A: To keep the resting membrane potential stable and prevent cramps
options.B: To seal the gap junctions and stop the spread of signals
options.C: To activate enzymes that cause the muscle fibers to shorten
options.D: To relax the muscle fibers by blocking electrical impulses

explanation: A surge in intracellular calcium triggers the chemical signals required for the uterine muscle fibers to shorten and contract effectively. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the term for the ability of uterine muscle fibers to stay partly shortened after each contraction?
explanation: Retraction is the progressive shortening of uterine muscle fibers during labor, which gradually pulls the cervix upward and prevents the baby from slipping back up. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does fundal dominance mean during normal labor?

options.A: The cervix contracts harder than the rest of the uterine wall
options.B: Uterine activity only happens during the second stage of labor
options.C: Contractions are strongest and last longest at the top of the uterus
options.D: The lower uterine segment does most of the pushing work

explanation: Fundal dominance ensures that the main pushing force is directed downward from the top of the uterus toward the birth canal. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which structural protein makes up most of a non-pregnant cervix?
explanation: Collagen provides the tough, fibrous support that keeps the cervix firm and closed throughout pregnancy. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which hormone keeps the cervix firm and tightly closed during most of pregnancy?
explanation: Progesterone dominance throughout pregnancy keeps the cervix firm and suppresses ripening until labor is near. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h4)

question: What term describes the process of the cervix thinning and shortening before birth?
explanation: Effacement refers to the gradual softening, shortening, and thinning of the cervix before and during early labor. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h5)

question: How do cervical changes usually differ between a first-time mother and a woman who has given birth before?

options.A: First-time mothers dilate twice as fast as women who have given birth before
options.B: Multiparas have zero changes in cervical length until pushing begins
options.C: First-time mothers usually efface the cervix completely before it dilates much
options.D: Multiparas complete all cervical dilatation before any effacement starts

explanation: In first-time mothers, the cervix typically thins out entirely first, whereas women who have given birth before often undergo effacement and dilatation at the same time. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which gland releases oxytocin into the bloodstream when the cervix stretches during labor?
explanation: Nerve impulses from the stretched cervix signal the brain, which causes the posterior pituitary gland to release stored oxytocin. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why is Ferguson's reflex considered a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Oxytocin production immediately stops the moment the cervix begins to dilate
options.B: Prostaglandins neutralize the hormones that cause the uterus to contract
options.C: Contractions cause cervical stretch, which releases more oxytocin to increase contractions
options.D: The mother's blood pressure drops to slow down the labor process

explanation: Positive feedback loops amplify the response, meaning stretching leads to oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions and more stretching. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is a normal contraction frequency during active first-stage labor?

options.A: Three to five contractions every ten minutes
options.B: One to two contractions every twenty minutes
options.C: Continuous cramping with no resting phase
options.D: Eight to ten contractions every five minutes

explanation: An effective active labor pattern typically consists of 3 to 5 contractions in a 10-minute window, leaving enough time for uterine relaxation and blood flow to the baby. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h7)

question: A midwife assesses a laboring woman and notices contractions lasting 60 seconds every 2 minutes with no resting time between them. What is the main concern here?

options.A: Exhaustion of the maternal posterior pituitary gland
options.B: Reduced blood flow and oxygen supply to the fetus
options.C: Premature rupture of the fetal membranes
options.D: Rapid cervical dilatation exceeding ten centimeters

explanation: Without a resting break between contractions, uterine blood vessels stay squeezed shut, cutting off oxygen exchange and risking fetal distress. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h7)
